question:
Patient note:
A 65-year-old retired machinist arrived at the emergency department by private vehicle at 04:30 after passing two toilets full of tar-black, glistening stool that clung stubbornly to the porcelain and stained the water a deep ink color beginning late the previous evening; he described an accompanying acrid, metallic odor that lingered in the bathroom and said he needed to flush repeatedly to clear the bowl. He has a twelve-year history of chronic hepatitis C genotype 1b acquired during military service and completed a direct-acting antiviral regimen three years ago, but follow-up imaging six months earlier still showed nodular liver morphology with mild portal venous enlargement and platelets in the 130 × 10⁹/L range; he takes nadolol 40 mg nightly as secondary prophylaxis after an episode of esophageal variceal bleeding two years prior, but he has not required lactulose, diuretics, or paracentesis and has never developed confusion or ascites. He denies alcohol since 2017, never used intravenous drugs, and quit a one-pack-per-day cigarette habit five years ago; medications otherwise include rosuvastatin 10 mg daily for dyslipidemia and a multivitamin, with no NSAIDs, aspirin, anticoagulants, or corticosteroids. He awoke at 23:00 with crampy mid-epigastric pressure and nausea but no vomiting; there was no hematemesis, no chest discomfort, no dyspnea, and at no point did his vision dim or the room spin, nor did he feel as though he might collapse. His last normal brown bowel movement had been the morning prior, and he recalls no recent change in diet, travel, antibiotic use, or abdominal trauma. Family history is relevant for a brother who required liver transplantation for hepatitis B–related cirrhosis; there is no known coagulopathy, coronary disease, or inflammatory bowel disease among relatives. Review of systems is negative for fevers, chills, night sweats, pruritus, jaundice beyond his baseline faint scleral tint, peripheral edema, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, urinary color change, or rash. On arrival—before any intravenous access, fluids, acid suppression, vasoactive therapy, blood products, or analgesics—he sat upright on the stretcher conversing coherently, skin warm and slightly pale but not diaphoretic. Manual vital signs obtained in triage documented a blood pressure of 120 / 72 mm Hg in the right arm at heart level, a regular pulse of 68 beats per minute corroborated on the monitor, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oral temperature 36.9 °C, and oxygen saturation 97 % breathing ambient air. Capillary refill was two seconds; conjunctivae were mildly anemic, sclerae carried subtle icterus, and oral mucosa was moist without petechiae. The neck was supple with flattened jugular veins at 30°, carotid upstrokes were brisk, and no peripheral edema was noted. Cardiac auscultation revealed a steady S1 and S2 with no murmurs, gallops, or rubs; lungs were clear to auscultation bilaterally. The abdomen was scaphoid, soft, and mildly tender over the epigastrium without guarding, rebound, or palpable masses; the liver edge was difficult to appreciate, and no splenic tip or ascites was detected by percussion or shifting dullness. Spider angiomas dotted the upper chest; there was faint palmar erythema but no digital clubbing or Dupuytren contracture. A focused neurologic screen showed full orientation, equal and reactive pupils, intact extra-ocular movements, and 5/5 strength throughout. Digital rectal examination produced copious dark, tarry stool that turned the guaiac card a deep blue within seconds. Two 18-gauge antecubital intravenous catheters were placed solely for laboratory draw at this juncture, and initial results available fifteen minutes later—still prior to any resuscitation—demonstrated hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL, hematocrit 32 %, mean corpuscular volume 91 fL, platelet count 138 × 10⁹/L, white blood cell count 7.4 × 10⁹/L, blood urea nitrogen 56 mg/dL, serum creatinine 1.0 mg/dL (baseline 0.9), sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, chloride 103 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, glucose 102 mg/dL, total bilirubin 1.5 mg/dL, albumin 3.2 g/dL, international normalized ratio 1.3, and aspartate and alanine aminotransferases mildly above upper normal limits. A 12-lead electrocardiogram obtained simultaneously showed normal sinus rhythm at 67 bpm with normal PR, QRS, and QT intervals and no ischemic ST-T changes. Upright chest radiography revealed clear lung fields and a normal cardiomediastinal silhouette; a supine abdominal film demonstrated a nonspecific gas pattern without pneumoperitoneum. At this precise clinical snapshot he had received no intravenous crystalloids, proton-pump inhibitor infusion, octreotide, antibiotics, or transfusion; he was kept nil per os, a type-and-screen was dispatched to the blood bank, continuous cardiac monitoring was initiated, and gastroenterology was paged for urgent esophagogastroduodenoscopy to identify and control the presumed upper gastrointestinal source of his maroon-black stool in the context of chronic viral liver injury with portal hypertensive sequelae.

Question: What is the patient's Glasgow-Blatchford Bleeding score? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
Glasgow-Blatchford Bleeding Score uses pretreatment labs, vital signs, presenting symptoms, and comorbidities:
- BUN 56 mg/dL corresponds to urea 20 mmol/L, in the 10 to <25 mmol/L band → 4.
- Hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL in a man, in the 10 to <12 g/dL band → 3.
- Systolic BP 120 mm Hg (≥110) → 0. Pulse 68/min (<100) → 0.
- Black tarry stool confirms melena → 1. No syncope → 0.
- Chronic liver disease with portal hypertension and prior variceal bleeding → 2. No heart failure → 0.
Total = 4 + 3 + 0 + 0 + 1 + 0 + 2 + 0 = 10.
Final answer: 10
